newsitem.title: USA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: BUSINESS PACKAGE THREATENED BY COLSTON UNCERTAINTY-REITH

Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says it would be a travesty if the Labor Party relied on Senator Colston's vote to defeat the Government's small business package in the Senate. Mr Reith says the Opposition has to commit itself not to take advantage of his Government's decision not to utilise Senator Colston's vote.
The Government's package includes legislation which will waive unfair dismissal laws for small business, a move which has been condemned by the Opposition.
CPSU GEARING UP FOR ANTI-GOVERNMENT CAMPAIGN
Mass union meetings will be held around Australia next Wednesday to endorse a campaign against further Federal Government industrial reforms.
The Community and Public Sector Union says government cuts and reforms to the public sector continue to threaten job security and conditions.
The Union's Wendy Caird says employment standards, which have been contained in central agreements for many years, are at risk and need to be protected during the reform process.
The CPSU in Canberra has launched an advertising campaign which could be extended nationally, to warn workers of the threat to their jobs under the Howard Government.
ABC CHIEF SAYS 500 MILLION FUNDING NECESSARY
The ABC says if the Government fails to give it the budget allocation of 500-million dollars recommended in the Mansfield report, it will be a repudiation of the review.
ABC chairman, Donald McDonald told ABC Radio, no area of ABC operations would be excluded from cuts if it doesn't receive the recommended amount.
Mr McDonald says the Corporation's board isn't prioritising where cuts will fall.
And he's warned that 500 million dollars will only provide domestic services, and maintenance of international broadcasting will cost more.
UNION PLANS TO ISOLATE WA DRAW CONDEMNATION FROM BUSINESS
Western Australia's unions and the ACTU have been accused of blackmail over their plans to isolate the state with a transport and communications boycott.
The unions plan widespread and continuing industrial action in response to the state government's new industrial relations laws, which passed through the lower house of Parliament yesterday.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry has condemned the campaign.
It says workers should look at the legislation for themselves and decide whether it's worth the loss of pay and the damage to the state's reputation.
The industrial action will disrupt interstate and local flights, freight, food deliveries, education and other services. - - - -
JURY RETIRES IN BRIAN QUINN CASE
The jury in the trial of fromer Coles Myer Chief, Brian Quinn, has retired to begin its deliberations.

Mr Quinn has pleaded not guilty to conspiring with the company's former head of maintenance, Graham Lanyon, to defraud Coles Myer of 4-point-6 million dollars, to pay for renovations to his Templestowe home.
The Supreme Court trial has been running for nine weeks.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
